suggestions.quote: Card, 2:58: in one study, most children aged three to eight who were told not to peek at a toy did, and lied about it; lying shows up around age two to three (c16, c08).
suggestions.fix: Card, 2:58: in developmental studies, most children aged three to eight who were told not to peek at a toy did, and lied about it, while lying first shows up around age two to three (c16, c08).

suggestions.quote: You expect a city lit up like a scoreboard, because you have heard you are lied to a hundred times a day. You get a city of dim zeros and ones, and a handful of heads blazing in the dozens: the five percent, and one of them is your boss.
suggestions.fix: You expect a city lit up like a scoreboard, because you have heard you are lied to a hundred times a day (c12). You get a city of dim zeros and ones, and a handful of heads blazing in the dozens: the five percent (c03, c04), and one of them is your boss.

suggestions.quote: Card, 1:58: in one 1996 diary study, adults from the community reported about one lie a day, students about two (c01).
suggestions.fix: Card, 1:58: across two 1996 diary studies, adults from the community reported about one lie a day, students about two (c01).

keep.quote: Card, 5:40: a 2012 press release claimed the nose warms when you lie; a 2017 study with thermal cameras found nose temperature tended to fall (c13, c18). [flat] "Nobody's nose is a counter."
Card, 6:25: in 2003 a National Research Council report found little scientific basis for expecting a polygraph to be extremely accurate, though specific-incident tests do better than chance (c09).

Card, 4:00: untrained people tell lies from truths about fifty-four percent of the time; they catch about forty-seven percent of lies and believe about sixty-one percent of truths (c06). [dry] "Everyone else is a coin flip that wants to believe you."
